lead: A schedule turns estimated effort into dated tasks, arranged in the order the work must happen. Estimation (see 6.3) says how much work exists; scheduling says when each piece starts and ends. The chain of tasks that fixes the finish date is the critical path, and it is what a project manager watches every week. Every plan, sprint board and release calendar is a schedule. Get the ordering wrong and the team is busy but late.
prereq: You need: effort and cost estimation from 6.3, plus the process models of Unit 1 to know which phases exist to be scheduled.

blocks.text: A work breakdown structure (WBS) splits the project into tasks small enough to estimate, assign and finish, usually one to ten person-days each. Each task then carries two different numbers. Effort is the total human work, counted in person-days. Duration is the space the task takes on the calendar, counted in working days.

Effort and duration are not the same. Two testers on a task estimated at 6 person-days need more than 3 days, because they must talk, share one build and wait for each other. Divide effort by people only when the work splits cleanly.

blocks.where: Effort is in person-days; People is the number assigned to the task; Duration is in working days. Add roughly 10–20% for coordination when People is more than 1.

items: Finish-to-start: B cannot start until A finishes. This is the common case.
Start-to-start: B may start once A has started, after some lag.
Finish-to-finish: B cannot finish until A finishes.
Start-to-finish: B cannot finish until A starts. Rare, used for some handovers.

blocks.text: Dependencies come from technology (testing needs code), from people (one database expert shared by two tasks) and from the customer (sign-off before release). Each dependency is an arrow in the schedule network.

sections.h3: Network, forward pass and the critical path

blocks.text: Tasks drawn as nodes with dependency arrows between them form a network. A path is any chain of tasks from the start of the project to its end. The project duration is the length of the longest path by duration, not the path with the most tasks. Two passes find it.

items: Forward pass: the earliest start (ES) of a task is the largest earliest finish among its predecessors; a task with no predecessor has ES = 0.
Project duration T = the largest EF anywhere in the network.
Backward pass from T: the latest finish (LF) of a task is the smallest latest start among its successors; for the last task, LF = T.
Slack of a task = LS − ES = LF − EF; tasks with zero slack are critical.

blocks.where: ES is earliest start, EF is earliest finish, LS is latest start, LF is latest finish, all in working days; Slack is the number of days the task can slip without moving the finish date.

blocks.text: The critical path is the chain of zero-slack tasks from start to finish. It controls the finish date: every day it slips, the project slips by one day. A task with slack can use those days freely, up to the slack, without touching the date.

blocks.where: O, M and P are the optimistic, most likely and pessimistic durations in days; E is the expected duration used in the network in place of a single guess. This is the PERT three-point estimate.

blocks.text: A Gantt chart draws one horizontal bar per task on a calendar axis. The bar starts at the earliest start, its length is the duration, and dependent bars sit end to end. Critical bars are usually coloured differently. Anyone can read it in ten seconds, which is why it appears in every status meeting.

Milestones are zero-duration markers for a finished event: design frozen, user acceptance signed off. They give checkpoints without pretending a review consumes no time. Level the schedule when one person is booked on two tasks in the same week; move the task with slack, never the critical one.

A schedule is a prediction, so it must be tracked. Every week, for each task, record the actual start, the actual finish if reached, and the remaining duration. Compare with the baseline. A task with 30% of its duration left and only two days before its latest finish needs action now: reassign people, cut scope, or accept a slip and re-plan the rest of the network.

Timeboxing reverses the usual logic: fix the end date, then fit the work inside it. If the box fills, drop the lowest-priority requirements instead of extending the date. An agile sprint of two to four weeks is a timebox. Report a slipping critical path into 6.5 as a project risk, and hand fixed release dates to 6.9.

examples.question: A module is broken into six tasks. A takes 3 days and starts first. B takes 4 days after A. C takes 2 days after A. D takes 5 days after B. E takes 3 days after C. F takes 2 days and starts after both D and E finish. Find the project duration, the critical path, and the slack of tasks C and E.
steps: Forward pass, task A: no predecessor, so ES = 0 and EF = 0 + 3 = 3 days.
Task B: ES = EF of A = 3, EF = 3 + 4 = 7 days. Task C: ES = 3, EF = 3 + 2 = 5 days.
Task D: ES = EF of B = 7, EF = 7 + 5 = 12 days. Task E: ES = EF of C = 5, EF = 5 + 3 = 8 days.
Task F has two predecessors: ES = max(EF of D, EF of E) = max(12, 8) = 12, EF = 12 + 2 = 14 days. Project duration T = 14 days.
Backward pass. F: LF = 14, LS = 14 − 2 = 12. D: LF = LS of F = 12, LS = 12 − 5 = 7. E: LF = 12, LS = 12 − 3 = 9.
B: LF = LS of D = 7, LS = 7 − 4 = 3. C: LF = LS of E = 9, LS = 9 − 2 = 7. A: LF = min(LS of B, LS of C) = min(3, 7) = 3, LS = 3 − 3 = 0.
The zero-slack chain is A, B, D, F, and its lengths add to 3 + 4 + 5 + 2 = 14 days, which matches T.
examples.answer: Project duration is 14 days; the critical path is A → B → D → F; tasks C and E each have 4 days of slack.

traps: Choosing the path with the most tasks. The critical path is the longest by duration; eight 1-day tasks take 8 days, two tasks of 5 days take 10.
Confusing effort with duration. A 20 person-day task with 2 people is not 20 days on the calendar, and it is usually more than 10.
Starting a task at the earlier predecessor's finish. With two predecessors, ES is the maximum of their earliest finishes, never the minimum or the average.
Adding slacks along one chain. Tasks in series share the same float, so two tasks showing 4 days each give the path 4 days, not 8.
Reading a Gantt bar's length as effort. The bar shows duration only; effort sits in the estimate behind it.

quiz.a: Critical path: the longest chain of dependent tasks from project start to finish; its length is the project duration. Slack: LS − ES, the days a task can slip without delaying the project.

quiz.q: Why is project duration the longest path by duration and not the path with the most tasks?
quiz.a: Paths run in parallel and the project ends when the last task ends, so the path with the largest total duration controls the finish. Six 1-day tasks take 6 days; two tasks of 4 days take 8.

quiz.q: A task has optimistic 2 days, most likely 4 days and pessimistic 12 days. Find its PERT expected duration.
Task X has two predecessors, ending on day 6 and day 9. X takes 4 days. Give its earliest start and earliest finish.
One critical task slips 3 days and one task with 5 days of slack slips 4 days. What happens to the finish date?
quiz.a: The critical slip moves the finish date by 3 days. The slack task uses 4 of its 5 days, so it does not affect the date but now has only 1 day of slack.

quiz.q: Two tasks in series each show 4 days of slack. Can you delay the path by 8 days?
quiz.a: No. Slack comes from the backward pass and tasks in series share the same float, so the path can slip 4 days only. Delaying both by 4 days already uses the full float.

quiz.q: Why is duration not exactly effort divided by people?
quiz.a: Extra people add communication, ramp-up, shared-build waiting and rework, so a 6 person-day task done by 2 people takes more than 3 days.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry extends the critical path method in three directions: resource levelling, which moves tasks so nobody is over-allocated; critical chain, which protects the plan with project and feeding buffers instead of per-task slack; and Monte Carlo schedule simulation, which samples task durations thousands of times to give a probability of finishing by a given date. Earned schedule tracks time rather than cost. Schedulers and agile boards implement these ideas, so the network maths stays the same underneath. Search for critical chain buffer management and Monte Carlo schedule risk analysis next.
